waypoints.name: White River Campground / Glacier Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trailhead at the upper D-loop of White River Campground; NPS climbing permit and self-issue wilderness camping permit required before heading up.
waypoints.directions: From Enumclaw, WA-410 runs about 43 miles east to the park's White River entrance; turn onto the Sunrise Road, cross the White River and turn onto the White River Road, following it to the campground at the end. Sort the climbing permit and the route-specific briefing before you drive up — both are required for this line — and check the road, which is seasonal.

waypoints.name: Glacier Basin
waypoints.note: End of maintained trail in a basin below the Inter Glacier moraine; a climbers' boot track continues cross-country from here toward St. Elmo Pass.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the Glacier Basin Trail from the upper campground loop and follow it up the White River valley, about 3.5 miles and 1,500 ft, crossing the West Fork on a footbridge. It is maintained the whole way and ends in the basin. Fill everything here: this is the last dependable running water until Camp Schurman on the way out.

waypoints.name: St. Elmo Pass
waypoints.note: Saddle between Steamboat Prow and Burroughs Mountain where the Liberty Ridge approach leaves the Inter Glacier basin and drops onto the Winthrop Glacier.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends at the basin. Leave it and climb snow and scree on an unsigned boot track up to the saddle, roughly 1,500 ft above. It can be hard ice early in the season and can cornice, so have the axe and crampons where you can reach them rather than buried in the pack.

waypoints.name: Winthrop Glacier traverse below Curtis Ridge
waypoints.note: Descend from St. Elmo Pass onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west beneath Curtis Ridge, roped for crevasses, toward the Carbon Glacier access ramp.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass onto the Winthrop and rope up — roped travel with crevasse-rescue gear is the standard from here on. Contour counter-clockwise around the mountain at roughly 7,300 to 7,400 ft, crossing longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats. Rockfall comes down right where you step onto the glacier, again mid-traverse, and again at its end, so this leg wants to be moved through early.

waypoints.name: Lower Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier camp
waypoints.note: Standard bivy on the flat at the base of the access ramp; next day cross the crevassed Carbon Glacier, weaving through open cracks, to reach the toe of Liberty Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Carry on around the toe of Curtis Ridge to the flat ground at the edge of the Carbon Glacier, where there is room for a couple of small tents. The whole traverse sits under Willis Wall and Ptarmigan Ridge, and both throw ice and rock more freely as the day warms.

waypoints.name: Thumb Rock
waypoints.note: Rock col/campsite on the ridge crest, the usual high camp before the summit push; exposed to rockfall and wind, so many parties dig in behind the rock.
waypoints.directions: Leave early enough to have the Carbon crossing behind you before the sun is on it. Drop onto the glacier and head south toward the toe of the ridge, negotiating the cracks, then start scouting a way onto the crest at somewhere around 8,600 to 8,800 ft. From there it is 30 to 40 degree snow with scrappy scree and rock steps up to the col. The camp is exposed to wind and to anything coming off the ridge above, so build a wall and pitch in the lee of the rock.

waypoints.name: Black Pyramid
waypoints.note: Steep 40-60° ice pitches and an exposed traverse onto the ridge's east face around this dark rock buttress; a rockfall and icefall hot spot, best climbed early/frozen.
waypoints.directions: Off in the small hours. From camp, either take the short steep ice step in the middle of the rock band directly or skirt the cliff by climbing up and to the left, then climb the ice gully between the rock walls, which can also be bypassed on its right. Above that the ridge steepens into sustained ice runnels. The whole stretch funnels rock and ice, so it wants to be climbed frozen and in the dark.

waypoints.name: Liberty Cap
waypoints.note: Liberty Ridge tops out on Liberty Cap's summit dome, the north sub-summit of Rainier overlooking Willis Wall; descend via the Emmons-Winthrop route past Camp Schurman.
waypoints.directions: Get past the Black Pyramid by moving onto the ridge’s east side, on exposed snow and ice up to about 60 degrees, with the angle easing back to 30 to 40 once you are around it. Several pitches of 40 to 60 degree ice and steep glacier ground then gain the Liberty Cap Glacier at around 13,500 ft. The bergschrund below the cap is usually the crux and varies year to year from a walk up a ramp to a short vertical ice step; the bridges and icy ledges across it are seasonal, so plan to climb it rather than count on finding a way over. Easier snow leads to the top.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small pullout on Cascade River Road ~21.7 mi from Marblemount; NW Forest Pass to park, self-issue wilderness permit required.
waypoints.directions: From SR-20 in Marblemount, take the Cascade River Road (FS Road 15) east about 22 miles. Pavement ends near mile 10; the gravel beyond is potholed and gets narrow and steep near the end. The Boston Basin trailhead is a small pullout at about 3,200 ft, just before the Cascade Pass road-end lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park, and camping in Boston Basin requires a park backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin
waypoints.directions: From the pullout, follow the old Diamond Mine roadbed about a mile, then take the unsigned climbers' path that leaves it and climbs steeply through forest, crossing four streams, to treeline near 5,300 ft. Continue up heather and boulder slopes into the Boston Basin cirque to the camps.

waypoints.name: West Ridge notch
waypoints.directions: Make an ascending traverse up and east across talus and the glacier remnant toward Forbidden's south face, roping up if it is snow-covered or crevassed; when it is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is often faster. Climb the obvious 500 ft snow couloir on the left edge of the south face, steepening to 40-50 degrees past a moat near the top, to the notch on the crest. Late season, use the loose Cat Scratch gullies just left of it.

waypoints.name: Forbidden Peak summit
waypoints.directions: From the notch, climb steep blocks onto the crest and follow it to climber's right over the air step and a series of gendarmes and knife edges, about six pitches of low fifth class. Take the crux tower two-thirds of the way up on its left side, continue along the narrowing crest to a false summit, downclimb about 10 ft of exposed rock, and make easy moves to the true summit.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive to Leavenworth and head up Icicle Creek Road, then turn onto Forest Road 7601 (signed as Eightmile Road) and follow it to its end, around 3,540 feet, where the Stuart Lake Trailhead and the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail begin.

waypoints.name: North Ridge Base
waypoints.directions: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake junction and stay right toward Stuart Lake. Where the trail later turns uphill and starts switchbacking away from Mountaineer Creek, leave it, cross the creek and follow the climbers' path up the valley, then climb loose talus into the basin under the Sherpa Glacier. Angle up the moraine to the lowest rock of the North Ridge at about 6,600 ft, with the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left.

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Fork Teanaway Road (FR-9737) to its end at the Esmeralda trailhead, about 4,243 ft, and start on the Ingalls Way Trail. At about 0.3 mile stay right onto Ingalls Way where it leaves the Esmeralda Basin Trail, and at about 1.7 miles turn right at the Longs Pass junction rather than carrying on toward Ingalls Basin. There is a longer northern approach to this ridge from the Stuart Lake Trailhead over Stuart Pass, but it adds significant mileage and is not the standard line, so Esmeralda is the lot you want.

waypoints.name: Longs Pass
waypoints.directions: From the signed Longs Pass junction on the Ingalls Way Trail, near 5,440 ft, turn right and climb steep, rocky, sparsely switchbacked trail about 1.2 miles to the pass, which gives the first clear view of Stuart's west side.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Last reliable water before the ridge; fill up here.
waypoints.directions: Descend the steep, dusty north side of the pass about a mile, losing about 1,300 ft, to Ingalls Creek in the timber and cross it. In normal summer flow it is a rock-hop; early in the season the slope above can hold snow and be icy at dawn.

waypoints.name: Talus Approach to West Ridge
waypoints.directions: After the creek, head west up the Ingalls Creek valley on the climbers' path toward Stuart Pass. Well short of the pass, in the upper meadows, leave the path and traverse north across talus and heather benches toward the foot of the West Ridge. There is no tread on this traverse, and several minor gullies look alike.

waypoints.name: West Ridge Crest
waypoints.directions: Aim for the deep middle gully of the three parallel gullies on the lower ridge, the one with a house-sized boulder at its foot. Push through scrub into it and scramble sandy class 3 granite up and rightward, with short class 4 steps, to the notch at its head where Long John Tower stands directly ahead. Snow can linger in the gully into midsummer and is often icy early in the day.

waypoints.name: Mount Stuart Summit
waypoints.directions: From the notch at the top of the approach gully, Long John Tower is directly ahead; pass it by the chimney on its left, or by the short dihedral with a fixed piton or the layback farther along the ledge, then regain the crest. Cross the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse, and higher up climb the 5.4 dihedral or 5.6 layback below the summit to easier fifth-class ground and the top.

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive to the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road, Forest Road 9737: from I-90 take exit 85 near Cle Elum onto SR 970 heading northeast, then follow the Teanaway River Road roughly 23 miles to the road-end parking at about 4,243 feet. The road is gravel and is not maintained through winter, typically staying snowed in until late June in a heavy year, so check conditions before an early-season trip.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Way Trail Junction
waypoints.directions: Walk the old road from the trailhead about 0.3 mile to the fork and bear right onto the Ingalls Way Trail, leaving the Esmeralda Basin Trail.

waypoints.name: Longs Pass
waypoints.directions: Climb the Ingalls Way Trail to the signed Longs Pass junction near 5,440 ft and turn right, then switchback up the open, shadeless hillside to the pass, where Mount Stuart and the Cascadian Couloir first come into view. Start before dawn in summer.

waypoints.name: Long's Pass Trail Junction
waypoints.directions: Descend the steep, loose trail down the north side of the pass, losing about 1,300 ft to Ingalls Creek, and cross the creek on the log to meet the Ingalls Creek Trail on the far bank. The slope can hold firm snow early in the season.

waypoints.name: Cascadian Couloir Base
waypoints.directions: Turn right (east, downstream) on the Ingalls Creek Trail and follow it a short way to an unmarked climbers' path on the left. Take it north through the meadow and camps to the toe of the couloir. Fill water here; none is reliable higher up.
